title: ERP Systems Explained in Under 8 Minutes
transcript: A lot of businesses wait until the last minute to figure out ERP. But don't worry, we're here to make it simple. Let's chat about what ERP software actually is, why it matters, and how you can tell if your business is ready for it. Hi, I'm Jeff Fyak with Software Connect. We help businesses find and evaluate software every day, and ERP is one of the most important systems to get right. So, what is ERP? ERP stands for enterprise resource planning. It's a software platform that combines all the important aspects of running your business. It manages finance, inventory, HR, customer management, and manufacturing or service management. Without an ERP, your teams are stuck in separate systems that don't talk to each other. No one in the business ever sees the full picture. However, with ERP, everyone from the warehouse to the boardroom is working off the same data. That's the highle definition. But to really understand ERP, we need to talk about where it came from. ERP started in 1960 when computers were just hitting the production lines. IBM and GLC Chase, a heavy equipment manufacturer, developed the first quote material resource planning software or MRP to track raw materials and manage production schedules. Back then, MRP was only for large manufacturers because the systems needed a lot of computing power to operate. As technology advanced, these systems added more tools for finance, purchasing, and maintenance management, laying the groundwork for ERP as we know it today. By the '90s, ERP systems started being used by organizations beyond manufacturing, helping all types of businesses. It was no longer just about managing production. It became a system for syncing operations across an entire organization. If you want a deeper dive into the backstory, check out our article on the evolution of ERP, linked below. So, what does an ERP actually do? Let's make it practical. Imagine you run a small but growing pet store. At first, you just need accounting to track income and expenses and pay vendors. The core of an ERP starts here, helping you automate bookkeeping and make tax time easier. As you add more to your product line, tracking stock gets tricky. You can't keep the right items in stock, and your spreadsheets become unmanageable. So, you need an inventory management. Next, you start hiring more staff, and you need to pay them accurately and on time. So you implement an HR and payroll system to track time, PTO, and deposit checks. Now you've grown large enough to start making your own line of treats. So you need a manufacturing software to trace ingredients, batches, and expiration dates. But you're also running promotions, tracking repeat customers, and handling support requests. So you need a CRM or marketing platform to manage customer data, email campaigns, and feedback, which are all disconnected from your current tech stack. At this point, you're juggling five different tools that don't talk to each other and start to feel a pain. Manually entering information from one system to the next, inconsistent data, and no clear view of how your company is performing. This is where ERP comes in. It combines all aspects of your business into one platform with unique modules for each workflow or department. So, when you sell a bag of dog food, inventory updates instantly. Revenue is recorded and sales data adjusts in real time. No more entering things twice. No more guessing. Everything is more or less automated. So, now that you know what ERP is and how it functions, let's talk about the different types of ERPs. ERP systems aren't all built the same. Some are cloud-based, some are on premise. Some are made for manufacturers, while others are made for service providers. A company's size, industry, and growth plans really determine what ERP fits best. Cloud ERPs are the most common option today. They're hosted online, accessible through a browser, and they're very scalable. Generally, they're offered as a monthly or yearly subscription and they're ideal for remote teams or multilocation businesses that want low IT overhead. On premise ERPs, on the other hand, are installed on your own servers. While you get full control of the system, you also take on the responsibility for maintenance and security. These are more common in large enterprises or highly regulated industries. And just as important as understanding how the software is deployed is understanding who the software is built for. ERP systems generally fall into three tiers based on the scale and complexity of the businesses they serve. Tier 1 ERPs like SAP S4 HANA and Oracle Cloud are designed for large multinational corporations. They support multiple entities, currencies, and global operations with deep customizations. But they also come with long implementation times and significant costs. Typically, they're best for Fortune 500 companies doing billions in annual revenue. Tier 2 ERPs like Netswuite, Acumatica, and Infor are targeted towards mid-market and growing companies. They're built for multi-ep department or multilocation organizations that need scalability or require industry specific tools like manufacturing or steel fabrication. These offer strong capabilities without the heavy footprint and price tag of tier 1 solutions. Tier 3 ERPs are more lightweight and modular, ideal for small businesses or startups. They focus on essentials like accounting, inventory or project tracking and often expand as the business grows. Some examples include ODO and Zoho 1. With integration tools like DigitBridge, even QuickBooks can extend its functionalities to act like a simple ERP platform. And for some larger companies, the choice is an eitheror. A tier 1 ERP may handle consolidated financials and compliance, while individual departments or subsidiaries run smaller tier 2 or three systems that better fit their day-to-day needs. This hybrid model gives enterprises top- down control without forcing every team into the same mold. So now that you understand the ERP landscape, how do you know if your business is actually ready to implement one? ERP selection is not something you rush. It's a detailed multi-step process. The system you choose will impact nearly every department in your company for years to come. Before looking at software and vendors, you'll need to align everyone internally, and you'll need to establish your primary business goals. It's not just about updating to the latest and greatest. First, figure out if you're trying to scale production, speed up accounting, or consolidate multiple systems. Also, you'll need to document your existing processes to see what's working and what's not. From there, you'll build a list of your must-haves. These include specific industry needs, integration with existing tools, compliance requirements, or mobile access, whatever your business truly needs to run. You should also consult with core stakeholders across your organization. Make sure to include personnel from finance, operations, IT, and leadership. Since ERP is really an operational decision, not just an IT call. Once your team is aligned and you know what your business needs, it's time to start researching and testing these systems. This is usually where many businesses hit a wall. There are hundreds, if not thousands of ERP systems on the market, each with its own features, strengths, and industry targets. How do you narrow down the short list to the ones your team should focus on? Comparing ERP apples to apples is almost impossible unless you've done it before. And that's where we come in. At Software Connect, we've spent over 20 years helping companies find the right ERP systems. We combine proprietary matching algorithms with software knowledge to narrow down your short list quickly so you don't waste months chasing down the wrong fit and testing platforms that will never work. And honestly, sometimes a full ERP isn't what you need. Maybe you need a new accounting platform or warehouse software that syncs with your existing setup. We can help you sort that out, too. ERP isn't just another piece of software. It's the backbone of your business's operation and competitiveness. If you found this video helpful, please like it and comment below.
